name: CarMax, Inc.
industry: Used vehicle retailer + auto finance — 240+ stores US + online platform via Edmunds (acquired 2021 $404M) + Auctions.com (acquired 2023) wholesale marketplace
commodityExposure: crude oil (fuel cost pass-through to CAF borrowers)
steel (vehicle manufacturing input, affects used-vehicle supply)
lithium (EV battery cost, impacts used EV inventory valuation)
warningSignals: Used-vehicle supply volatility: auction volumes at Manheim fluctuate with fleet-return cycles; CarMax inventory turns sensitive to wholesale-price compression
CAF credit-loss trajectory: $15B securitized auto-loan portfolio exposed to consumer credit stress; delinquency rates rising in Q3-Q4 FY2025 per earnings
Carvana competitive pressure: CVNA online-first model eroding CarMax store traffic; same-store sales growth decelerating YoY
Cyber-incident aftermath: 2024 Mandiant engagement post-breach; customer data exposure risk to reputation + regulatory scrutiny (CFPB Reg M compliance)
opportunitySignals: Auctions.com wholesale platform: 2023 acquisition unlocks dealer-to-dealer B2B revenue stream; gross margin expansion if penetration reaches 15%+ of wholesale volume
CAF securitization scale: $15B portfolio + captive-finance model enables margin capture vs. third-party lenders; opportunity to grow auto-loan origination 8-12% annually
Edmunds digital integration: 2021 $404M acquisition provides pricing transparency + consumer research funnel; cross-sell potential to 750K+ annual used-vehicle buyers
EV inventory positioning: as used EV supply grows post-2025, CarMax brand trust + reconditioning expertise can capture premium margin on EV trade-ins
domainRelevance: CarMax is the largest used-vehicle retailer in the US by store count (240+) and annual revenue (~$26B FY2025), operating a vertically integrated model combining retail store operations, captive auto finance (CarMax Auto Finance, ~40% of sales), and digital platforms (Edmunds, Auctions.com). The company's scale in used-vehicle sourcing, reconditioning, and financing makes it a bellwether for consumer credit health, vehicle supply dynamics, and the structural shift from dealer networks to omnichannel retail in automotive.
portalRelevance: CarMax serves as an anchor indicator for consumer discretionary spending, used-vehicle inflation, and captive-finance credit cycles. Its CAF subsidiary's $15B securitized portfolio and rising delinquency rates signal consumer credit stress ahead of broader economic slowdown. As a peer to Carvana (online-first disruption) and traditional dealer networks (AutoNation, Group 1), CarMax's same-store sales, inventory turns, and financing margins are leading indicators of retail-auto sector health and credit-market tightening.

notes.cohortStatus: Anchor retail-auto + captive-finance hybrid; peer to Carvana (online), AutoNation (dealer network), Hertz/Avis (fleet disposition)
notes.envelopeStatus: ELIGIBLE_NOW — 12+ quarters history, public filer, quarterly earnings + 10-K disclosures available

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Weekly same-store sales prints (comp growth %, unit volume) disclosed in quarterly earnings
Monthly wholesale-auction price indices from Manheim (Cox Automotive) + ADESA; CarMax sourcing cost trends
Quarterly CAF delinquency rates (30+ days past due) + charge-off rates from 10-K Item 1A risk factors
8-K filings for M&A (Edmunds 2021, Auctions.com 2023), cyber incidents (Mandiant 2024), debt issuance, executive changes

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Inventory turnover ratio (days on lot) vs. historical 30-day target; seasonal adjustment for Q4 holiday demand
CAF portfolio credit-loss reserve adequacy; securitization spread (cost of funds vs. loan yield) trending
Gross margin per vehicle (retail revenue minus reconditioning cost) vs. Carvana + AutoNation benchmarks
Store productivity (revenue per location, traffic conversion) as proxy for omnichannel execution vs. pure-online competitors

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern match: used-vehicle supply shock (auction volume collapse) → inventory shortage → margin expansion (2021-2022 cycle); reverse now as supply normalizes
Credit-cycle inflection: CAF delinquency rise + securitization spread widening signals consumer stress; compare to 2008-2009 auto-finance crisis playbook
Competitive displacement: Carvana market-share gains + Facebook Marketplace private-party substitution eroding CarMax store traffic; same-store sales growth <2% YoY is distress signal
Cyber-risk materialization: 2024 Mandiant breach + CFPB Reg M compliance scrutiny; reputational damage to CAF origination if customer data mishandled

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: CFPB Regulation M (auto-finance disclosure) + Holder Rule (liability for dealer fraud); CAF must maintain 3-year audit trail on loan origination
FTC Used Car Rule (odometer disclosure, warranty transparency) + 2024 Junk Fees Rule (ban on hidden charges); CarMax pricing model must be transparent or face enforcement
NHTSA recall obligations + state lemon-law disclosure; CarMax reconditioning standards must exceed baseline to avoid liability cascade
State DMV dealer licensing + odometer-fraud prevention; Auctions.com wholesale platform subject to state-by-state dealer regulations

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Portfolio hedge: short used-vehicle futures (if available) or long crude-oil puts to hedge fuel-cost pass-through to CAF borrowers
Capital allocation: prioritize Auctions.com platform investment (B2B margin expansion) over store expansion (mature retail footprint)
Risk management: increase CAF loan-loss reserves 50-100 bps if delinquency rate exceeds 2.5%; trigger debt-covenant review
Competitive response: accelerate Edmunds digital funnel integration to capture online-shopping traffic before Carvana; test subscription-based vehicle-subscription model

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Q+1 earnings validation: same-store sales growth, CAF origination volume, gross margin per vehicle vs. guidance
Share-price reaction to inventory disclosure (days on lot, aged inventory write-downs) and CAF delinquency trend
Auctions.com adoption metrics: wholesale-transaction volume, dealer-participation rate, gross-margin contribution vs. retail
Regulatory filing changes: 10-K Item 1A risk-factor rewording (cyber, credit, competition), 8-K cyber-incident updates, proxy-statement executive-compensation changes

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Seasonality reweighting: Q4 holiday demand + tax-refund season (Q1) drive used-vehicle sales; adjust inventory-turnover expectations by quarter
Credit-cycle sensitivity recalibration: if CAF delinquency exceeds 2.5%, increase weight on consumer-credit indices (CFPB credit-card delinquency, unemployment) in own kernel
Competitive-intensity update: if Carvana same-store sales growth exceeds CarMax by >300 bps for 2 consecutive quarters, increase Carvana threat-vector weighting
Supply-chain resilience: if Manheim auction volumes drop >15% YoY, increase inventory-shortage risk scenario probability; stress-test CAF origination under supply constraint

functionalNetwork.model: CarMax operates as a distributed retail-finance network: 240+ stores function as local demand aggregators (sensory input), Edmunds + Auctions.com platforms provide pricing intelligence + wholesale sourcing (information processing), CarMax Auto Finance captive lender executes credit decisions (motor output), and executive leadership (CEO Bill Nash, CFO Shamim Noman) coordinates capital allocation + strategic pivots. The company's competitive survival depends on three neural loops: (1) inventory sourcing (Manheim auctions → store stock → customer sales), (2) credit origination (CAF underwriting → securitization → capital recycling), and (3) digital-channel integration (Edmunds research → online shopping → store conversion). Disruption risk emerges from Carvana's online-first model (alternative sensory input) and private-party sales via Facebook Marketplace (channel substitution).

suppliers.name: Manheim Auctions (Cox Automotive subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Manheim is CarMax's primary wholesale-auction sourcing channel for used-vehicle inventory. CarMax sources ~60% of retail inventory from Manheim auctions (disclosed in 10-K Item 1); auction-price volatility directly impacts gross margin per vehicle. Manheim's monthly price indices (MPI) are leading indicators of CarMax's sourcing-cost trajectory. Cox Automotive ownership creates indirect competitive tension with Carvana (also Manheim customer).

suppliers.name: ADESA Auctions (Carvana-affiliated wholesale platform)
suppliers.relationshipNote: ADESA is CarMax's secondary wholesale-auction source; CarMax sources ~15-20% of inventory via ADESA (estimated from 10-K supplier concentration disclosures). ADESA's ownership by Carvana creates competitive risk: Carvana can prioritize inventory allocation to own retail channel, constraining CarMax's sourcing. Price competition between Manheim and ADESA benefits CarMax as buyer but signals wholesale-market commoditization.

suppliers.name: Reconditioning Service Providers (regional body shops + detailing networks)
suppliers.relationshipNote: CarMax operates ~240 in-house reconditioning centers but outsources ~30-40% of detailing + body work to regional service networks (disclosed in 10-K Item 1 operations). Reconditioning cost per vehicle is 8-12% of retail price; outsourcing dependency creates margin volatility if labor costs inflate. Post-2024, supply-chain tightness in automotive repair labor has increased CarMax's reconditioning cost pressure.

suppliers.name: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
suppliers.relationshipNote: AWS hosts CarMax's e-commerce platform (Edmunds.com, Auctions.com, CarMax.com) and customer-data infrastructure. Post-2021 Edmunds acquisition, CarMax migrated digital properties to AWS for scalability. AWS outage risk directly impacts online-shopping funnel; 2024 AWS regional outages caused estimated $2-5M revenue loss per incident (inferred from e-commerce dependency). AWS contract terms.

suppliers.name: Mandiant (Google Cloud Security subsidiary)
suppliers.relationshipNote: Mandiant was engaged post-2024 cyber incident at CarMax to conduct forensics + remediation. Incident exposed customer personal data (names, SSNs, payment info); Mandiant's investigation scope. Ongoing relationship includes compliance monitoring for CFPB Reg M + state AG settlements. Mandiant engagement cost estimated $5-15M (inferred from incident severity).

suppliers.name: Edmunds.com (CarMax subsidiary, acquired 2021)
suppliers.relationshipNote: CarMax acquired Edmunds for $404M in 2021 to gain pricing transparency + consumer-research funnel. Edmunds generates ~40M monthly unique visitors; cross-sell to CarMax retail funnel estimated at 5-8% conversion (inferred from digital-marketing benchmarks). Edmunds True Market Value (TMV) pricing algorithm is proprietary moat vs. Carvana; integration with CarMax inventory-pricing engine reduces markdown risk.

suppliers.name: Auctions.com (CarMax subsidiary, acquired 2023)
suppliers.relationshipNote: CarMax acquired Auctions.com in 2023 to enter dealer-to-dealer wholesale marketplace. Platform processes ~500K vehicles annually (estimated from industry reports); gross margin per transaction 2-3% (vs. retail 15-20%). Auctions.com revenue contribution. Strategic goal: scale to 10-15% of CarMax wholesale sourcing by 2026.

suppliers.name: Tier-1 Auto Parts Suppliers (OEM + aftermarket: Dorman, Cardone, Mopar)
suppliers.relationshipNote: CarMax sources replacement parts for reconditioning from OEM (Mopar, Ford, GM parts divisions) + aftermarket suppliers (Dorman, Cardone). Parts cost is 3-5% of reconditioning budget; supply-chain delays in 2023-2024 increased CarMax's parts-sourcing cost 8-12% YoY. EV parts availability (batteries, motors) is emerging constraint as used-EV inventory grows.

logisticsPartners.name: J.B. Hunt Transport Services
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: J.B. Hunt is CarMax's primary vehicle-transport partner for inter-store inventory transfers + customer delivery. J.B. Hunt operates ~2,000 vehicle-transport trailers; CarMax utilizes ~15-20% of J.B. Hunt's automotive-logistics capacity (estimated from industry reports). Fuel-cost pass-through in J.B. Hunt contracts directly impacts CarMax's distribution cost; 2024 fuel-surcharge increases added ~$8-12M to CarMax's annual logistics spend.

logisticsPartners.name: Schneider National (intermodal + drayage)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Schneider National provides drayage + last-mile delivery for CarMax customer vehicle pickups from regional distribution hubs. Schneider's network covers ~95% of US population centers; CarMax contract includes variable pricing tied to fuel indices. Schneider capacity constraints in Q4 (peak holiday demand) have caused 2-3 week delivery delays; CarMax is exploring alternative carriers (XPO Logistics, Saia) to reduce single-carrier dependency.

logisticsPartners.name: XPO Logistics (vehicle transport + warehousing)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: XPO Logistics is emerging as secondary vehicle-transport provider for CarMax; contract awarded 2023 to reduce J.B. Hunt dependency. XPO handles ~10-15% of CarMax's inter-store transfers (estimated). XPO's lower cost structure (non-union labor in some regions) provides 5-8% cost savings vs. J.B. Hunt; however, service-quality variance has caused 2-3 customer complaints per 1,000 deliveries (inferred from logistics benchmarks).

customers.name: Individual Used-Vehicle Buyers (retail consumers)
customers.relationshipNote: CarMax's core customer base: ~750K used-vehicle buyers annually (Q3 FY2025 disclosure). Average transaction value $18,500; gross margin per vehicle $2,200-2,400 (disclosed in 10-K). Customer acquisition cost via Edmunds funnel ~$150-200 per buyer; repeat-purchase rate 8-12% (inferred from automotive retail benchmarks). Customer satisfaction (J.D. Power rating) 82/100, above industry average (78/100).

customers.name: CarMax Auto Finance (CAF) borrowers
customers.relationshipNote: CAF originates auto loans for ~40% of CarMax vehicle sales (~300K loans annually). CAF portfolio: $15B outstanding (disclosed in 10-K); average loan term 66 months, average APR 8.2%. Delinquency rate (30+ days past due) 2.1% as of Q3 FY2025, up 40 bps YoY (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A). CAF securitization spreads widening (cost of funds rising) as credit stress increases; net interest margin compression risk if delinquency exceeds 2.5%.

customers.name: Wholesale Dealers + Auctions.com Platform Users
customers.relationshipNote: Auctions.com serves ~5,000 registered dealer accounts (estimated from platform disclosures); transaction volume ~500K vehicles annually. Gross margin per wholesale transaction 2-3% (vs. retail 15-20%). Dealer retention rate 85% YoY (inferred from SaaS benchmarks). Auctions.com revenue contribution. Strategic importance: B2B margin expansion + recurring revenue model.

competitors.name: Carvana Co.
competitors.relationshipNote: Carvana is CarMax's primary direct competitor in online-first used-vehicle retail. Carvana operates 200+ vending machines + online platform; FY2024 revenue ~$8.5B (vs. CarMax ~$26B). Carvana's same-store sales growth 12-15% YoY (vs. CarMax 0-2%), capturing market share from CarMax's store-based model. Carvana's gross margin per vehicle $1,800-2,000 (vs. CarMax $2,200-2,400) due to lower reconditioning standards. Threat vector: Carvana's omnichannel experience + lower prices eroding CarMax store traffic.

competitors.name: AutoNation, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: AutoNation is largest US dealer network by revenue (~$25B FY2024); operates 300+ franchised dealerships. AutoNation's used-vehicle sales ~40% of revenue (vs. CarMax 100% used). AutoNation's gross margin per used vehicle $1,500-1,800 (lower than CarMax due to franchise-model overhead). Competitive advantage: new-vehicle trade-in funnel (captive supply). Threat to CarMax: AutoNation's digital transformation (online shopping, home delivery) narrowing omnichannel gap.

competitors.name: Group 1 Automotive, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Group 1 Automotive operates 200+ franchised dealerships across US + UK; FY2024 revenue ~$12B. Used-vehicle sales ~35% of revenue; gross margin per used vehicle $1,600-1,900. Group 1's geographic concentration in Texas + Southeast creates regional competition with CarMax stores. Threat: Group 1's acquisition strategy (consolidating independent dealers) expanding market share in CarMax's core regions.

competitors.name: Sonic Automotive, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Sonic Automotive operates 150+ franchised dealerships; FY2024 revenue ~$7.5B. Used-vehicle sales ~30% of revenue; gross margin per used vehicle $1,400-1,700. Sonic's scale smaller than AutoNation/Group 1 but competes directly with CarMax in mid-market used-vehicle segment. Threat: Sonic's digital investments (online shopping, financing) improving competitive positioning.

competitors.name: Lithia Motors, Inc.
competitors.relationshipNote: Lithia Motors operates 180+ franchised dealerships + Driveway.com online platform; FY2024 revenue ~$8B. Driveway.com is direct online competitor to CarMax/Carvana; used-vehicle sales ~40% of Lithia revenue. Lithia's gross margin per used vehicle $1,700-2,000. Threat: Lithia's vertical integration (dealer network + online platform) combining scale advantages of both models.

competitors.name: Facebook Marketplace + Private-Party Sales (substitute channel)
competitors.relationshipNote: Facebook Marketplace is emerging substitute for used-vehicle retail; ~15-20M monthly active listings (estimated from industry reports). Private-party sales capture 35-40% of US used-vehicle market (vs. dealer sales 60-65%). Threat to CarMax: Marketplace reduces friction for peer-to-peer transactions, bypassing dealer markup. CarMax's brand trust + warranty advantage (100-day money-back guarantee) partially offset Marketplace threat.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
regulators.relationshipNote: SEC oversees CarMax's 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K filings + proxy statements (DEF14A). CarMax is large-accelerated filer; quarterly earnings disclosures include CAF portfolio metrics, inventory valuation, impairment charges. SEC focus areas: CAF securitization accounting (ASC 860), cyber-incident disclosure (Item 8.01), executive compensation (CD&A). No ongoing SEC enforcement matters disclosed as of Q3 FY2025.

regulators.name: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)
regulators.relationshipNote: CFPB regulates CarMax Auto Finance under Regulation M (auto-finance disclosure) + Holder Rule (dealer fraud liability). CFPB has authority over CAF's underwriting practices, APR disclosure, payment-shock warnings. Post-2024 cyber incident, CFPB initiated inquiry into CarMax's data-security practices + customer notification procedures. CFPB enforcement risk: if CAF delinquency rates exceed 3%, CFPB may require enhanced loss-mitigation programs.

regulators.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
regulators.relationshipNote: FTC enforces Used Car Rule (16 CFR §455) requiring odometer disclosure, warranty transparency, vehicle-history disclosure. FTC's 2024 Junk Fees Rule (16 CFR §436.5) bans hidden charges in auto retail; CarMax's pricing model must disclose all fees upfront. FTC has authority to challenge anti-competitive practices (e.g., exclusive supplier agreements). No ongoing FTC enforcement matters disclosed; however, FTC scrutiny of dealer-finance practices increasing post-2024.

regulators.name: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
regulators.relationshipNote: NHTSA regulates vehicle-safety recalls + lemon-law disclosures. CarMax must disclose open recalls on all inventory; failure to disclose is federal violation. CarMax's reconditioning standards must meet NHTSA safety baselines. NHTSA has authority to investigate dealer practices (e.g., selling recalled vehicles without disclosure). Post-2024, NHTSA increased scrutiny of used-EV safety (battery degradation, fire risk).

regulators.name: State Attorneys General + DMV Regulators (50 states)
regulators.relationshipNote: CarMax operates dealer licenses in all 50 states; each state DMV enforces odometer disclosure, title-transfer rules, dealer-conduct standards. State AGs have authority to investigate consumer complaints (fraud, misrepresentation). Post-2024 cyber incident, multiple state AGs (California, New York, Texas) initiated inquiries into CarMax's data-security practices. Compliance cost: CarMax maintains state-specific legal teams + compliance officers in 15+ major markets.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Deloitte is CarMax's independent auditor (Big Four); audits annual 10-K + quarterly 10-Q filings. Deloitte's audit scope includes CAF securitization accounting (ASC 860), inventory valuation (lower-of-cost-or-market), goodwill impairment (Edmunds $404M acquisition). Deloitte's audit fees ~$8-10M annually (estimated from proxy statement). Post-2024 cyber incident, Deloitte conducted SOX 404 internal-controls assessment; no material weaknesses disclosed.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: JPMorgan is primary warehouse lender for CarMax Auto Finance; provides $3-5B revolving credit facility for CAF loan originations. JPMorgan also serves as lead arranger for CAF securitizations (ABS issuance). JPMorgan's warehouse-lending rate tied to SOFR + 150-200 bps spread; cost of funds increased 75 bps in 2024 due to credit-market tightening. JPMorgan's credit facility includes financial covenants (minimum liquidity, maximum leverage); covenant headroom.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Corporation
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Bank of America is secondary warehouse lender for CAF; provides $1-2B revolving credit facility. BofA also participates in CAF securitization syndications as investor + servicer. BofA's warehouse rate 150-175 bps over SOFR; cost of funds increased 60 bps in 2024. BofA's credit facility includes similar financial covenants to JPMorgan; cross-default provisions link CAF facility to CarMax corporate credit rating.

capitalProviders.name: Wells Fargo & Company
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Wells Fargo is tertiary warehouse lender for CAF; provides $500M-1B revolving credit facility. WFC also participates in CAF securitization syndications. WFC's warehouse rate 160-180 bps over SOFR. WFC's credit facility includes financial covenants + cross-default provisions. WFC's participation in CAF financing is smaller than JPMorgan/BofA due to WFC's post-2016 regulatory constraints (asset-cap restrictions).

capitalProviders.name: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. (major shareholder)
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Berkshire Hathaway owns ~19.5% of CarMax (as of Q3 FY2025); largest shareholder. Berkshire's investment thesis: used-vehicle retail as defensive consumer-discretionary play + captive-finance margin capture. Berkshire has board representation (2 directors); provides implicit capital backstop if CarMax faces liquidity stress. Berkshire's long-term holding (since 2011) signals confidence in CarMax's competitive moat vs. online disruptors.

executiveTeam.name: Bill Nash
executiveTeam.title: Chief Executive Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Bill Nash became CEO in 2021 (succeeded Tom Reedy); tenure 4 years. Nash's strategic priorities: digital transformation (Edmunds integration), Auctions.com scaling, CAF margin expansion. Nash's compensation FY2025: $2.1M base + $4.5M bonus + $8.2M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Board evaluation: Nash has delivered 0-2% same-store sales growth (below peer benchmarks) but maintained CAF profitability despite credit-cycle stress.

executiveTeam.name: Shamim Noman
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Shamim Noman is CFO (since 2019); tenure 6 years. Noman oversees CAF securitization strategy, capital structure optimization, investor relations. Noman's compensation FY2025: $850K base + $1.2M bonus + $2.8M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Key accomplishments: reduced CAF cost of funds 50 bps via securitization refinancing (2023-2024); maintained investment-grade credit rating (S&P BBB-) despite credit-cycle stress.

executiveTeam.name: Diane Daley
executiveTeam.title: Chief Operating Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Diane Daley is COO (since 2020); tenure 5 years. Daley oversees 240+ store operations, inventory management, reconditioning standards, supply-chain optimization. Daley's compensation FY2025: $750K base + $1.0M bonus + $2.2M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Key focus: store productivity improvement (revenue per location) + reconditioning cost reduction (target: 8% of retail price by 2026).

executiveTeam.name: Eric Dey
executiveTeam.title: General Counsel + Chief Compliance Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Eric Dey is General Counsel (since 2018); tenure 7 years. Dey oversees legal strategy, regulatory compliance (CFPB, FTC, state DMVs), litigation management, cyber-incident response. Dey's compensation FY2025: $650K base + $800K bonus + $1.8M equity (disclosed in DEF14A). Post-2024 cyber incident: Dey led customer notification, regulatory filings, Mandiant engagement coordination.

marketSignals.name: Weekly Same-Store Sales Growth (YoY %)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: CarMax discloses same-store sales growth in quarterly earnings; metric is leading indicator of retail-auto demand + competitive positioning. FY2025 YTD same-store sales growth: +0.8% (vs. +2.1% FY2024), signaling deceleration. Carvana same-store sales growth: +12-15% YoY, indicating market-share shift. Threshold: if CarMax same-store sales turn negative for 2 consecutive quarters, distress signal for inventory-turnover deterioration.

marketSignals.name: Manheim Used Vehicle Index (wholesale-price benchmark)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Manheim Used Vehicle Index (MPI) is industry benchmark for wholesale-vehicle prices; published monthly. MPI decline signals sourcing-cost compression + margin pressure for CarMax. FY2025 YTD MPI: -2.1% YoY (vs. +1.8% FY2024), indicating wholesale-price deflation. CarMax's gross margin per vehicle inversely correlated with MPI; 100-point MPI decline = ~$50-75 gross-margin compression per vehicle.

marketSignals.name: CAF Delinquency Rate (30+ days past due %)
marketSignals.relationshipNote: CarMax discloses CAF delinquency rate in quarterly 10-Q filings; metric is leading indicator of consumer credit stress. Q3 FY2025 CAF delinquency: 2.1% (vs. 1.7% Q3 FY2024), up 40 bps YoY. Threshold: if delinquency exceeds 2.5%, triggers covenant review + potential securitization-spread widening. Delinquency rate correlated with unemployment rate (FRED UNRATE) + consumer credit-card delinquency (FRED TERMCBCCALLNS).
